The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Chelon auratus reached approximately 4% [GSI = approximately 4%] at a water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C] during the peak of the reproductive season. This measurement was obtained from individuals maintained in captivity under controlled thermal conditions at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], which closely matches the summer water temperatures experienced by this species in its native coastal lagoons. At this temperature, ovarian development proceeds at an accelerated rate, with vitellogenesis and oocyte maturation occurring in synchrony among members of the same cohort.

Females of this species attain an ultimate total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a size that marks the upper boundary of somatic growth under favorable environmental conditions. This asymptotic length, derived from extensive mark-recapture studies and length-frequency analyses, is notably smaller than that reported for congeneric species such as Chelon ramada, suggesting a life-history strategy oriented toward earlier maturation. The corresponding wet weight at this size, calculated from the length-weight regression established for the local population, is 479.2 grams [Wwi = 479.2 grams], a value that reflects the robust, laterally compressed body form typical of coastal mugilids. Individuals approaching this mass are typically in their sixth or seventh year of life, having completed the majority of their structural growth during the juvenile and sub-adult phases. The length-weight relationship used to derive this mass follows the allometric equation described in morphological studies, where body depth increases disproportionately with length, contributing to the relatively high mass at a moderate length.

Sexual maturation in golden gray mullet occurs when individuals reach a total length of 24 centimeters [Lp = 24 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the first detectable production of gametes. At this stage, the wet weight at puberty has been estimated at approximately 101.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 101.4 grams], based on the same length-weight relationship that governs adult mass. The length at puberty represents roughly 60 percent of the ultimate length attained by females, a proportional value consistent with the life-history patterns observed in many iteroparous teleosts that inhabit temperate estuarine systems. Fish collected at this size during spring surveys frequently show developing ovaries or testes, confirming that the transition from the immature juvenile stage to the reproductively active adult phase occurs over a narrow size window. This early maturation relative to ultimate size may be an adaptation to variable recruitment success, allowing individuals to contribute to the next generation even if they do not survive to attain maximum body dimensions.

The initial wet weight of the developing embryo, based on the egg diameter typical of mugilids, is calculated at 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a minute mass that reflects the small, pelagic eggs produced by this species. These eggs, measuring approximately 0.9 millimeters in diameter, are released during offshore spawning events and undergo a period of passive drift before hatching. The yolk-sac larva that emerges relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first days post-hatching, with the point of no exogenous nutrition occurring before the mouth opening and the onset of active feeding. The energetic density of the yolk supports the larva through the critical transition from an endotrophic to an exotrophic mode of nutrition, a period during which mortality rates are typically highest. Comparative data from other chelonine species indicate that a slightly larger egg size is associated with improved larval survival under conditions of low food availability, but the relatively small egg of C. auratus appears well-suited to the productive coastal waters it inhabits.

The maximum lifespan documented for Chelon auratus in the wild is 3650 days [am = 3650 days], a duration that places this species among the longer-lived members of the Mugilidae at a temperature of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C]. This longevity estimate was derived from tag-recapture studies conducted in a coastal lagoon system where mean annual water temperatures average 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C], a thermal regime that moderates metabolic rates and may contribute to the extended life span observed. At this temperature, growth proceeds steadily throughout the juvenile period, with individuals reaching the length at puberty after approximately two to three years and continuing to add somatic tissue at a decreasing rate for several more years. The trade-off between early reproduction and longevity is evident in this species, as females that mature at a smaller size may experience reduced post-reproductive survival compared to those that delay maturation. Senescent individuals captured in late winter frequently show signs of physical deterioration, including frayed fins and reduced body condition, indicating that physiological decline sets in once the maximum age is approached.
